title: Penguin Body Mass Distribution
text:
This post explores the body mass of penguins using Python.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: Penguin Body Mass Distribution
text:
Setup
We start by importing our necessary Python libraries and loading the dataset.

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()


avg_mass = penguins.groupby('species')['body_mass_g'].mean().reset_index()
avg_mass.columns = ['Species', 'Average Mass (g)']

print(avg_mass)

     Species  Average Mass (g)
0     Adelie       3700.662252
1  Chinstrap       3733.088235
2     Gentoo       5076.016260



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.boxplot(data=penguins, x='species', y='body_mass_g')
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Body Mass (g)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass distribution of penguins by species.

title: Analyzing Penguin Bill Dimensions
text:
This post explores the Palmer Penguins dataset using R.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: Analyzing Penguin Bill Dimensions
text:
Setup
We load the necessary libraries, suppressing startup messages and warnings.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)


clean_penguins <- penguins |> drop_na()
head(clean_penguins)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
5 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>



ggplot(clean_penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Bill Length (mm)", y = "Bill Depth (mm)")







Figure 1: Scatterplot of bill length vs. bill depth by species.

title: Bonus: R and Python Integration
text: This post demonstrates passing data between R and Python using the reticulate package in a single Quarto document.

title: Bonus: R and Python Integration
text:
Setup
First, we load reticulate and point it to the project’s uv virtual environment so it uses the correct Python installation.

library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("../../.venv", required = TRUE)

title: Bonus: R and Python Integration
text:
Create Data in Python
Let’s generate a simple Pandas DataFrame in Python. Notice how we use {python} to tell Quarto to switch languages here.

import pandas as pd

python_data = {
    'species': ['Adelie', 'Chinstrap', 'Gentoo'],
    'count': [152, 68, 124]
}
python_df = pd.DataFrame(python_data)
print(python_df)

     species  count
0     Adelie    152
1  Chinstrap     68
2     Gentoo    124



library(ggplot2)

# Access the Python object
r_df <- py$python_df

ggplot(r_df, aes(x = species, y = count, fill = species)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Penguin Counts (Data from Python, Plot from R)",
       x = "Species", y = "Count")







Figure 1: Penguin counts by species, plotted in R from Python data.
